title: Synergistic effects of traffic-related air pollution and exposure to violence on urban asthma etiology.
ehr_evidence: We employ data from the Maternal-Infant Smoking Study of East Boston (MISSEB), a community-based prospective pregnancy cohort examining asthma, respiratory, and cognitive development; exposures were estimated via passive NO2 monitoring and GIS/land-use regression models, and exposure to violence was assessed through caregiver questionnaires.
summary: In a community-based prospective pregnancy cohort of 413 children in East Boston, Massachusetts (recruited 1987–1993), lifetime exposure to violence (ETV) modified the association between traffic-related NO2 and childhood asthma, with elevated risk confined to children with above-median ETV.
key_findings: A 1-SD (4.3 ppb) increase in year-of-diagnosis NO2 was associated with elevated odds of asthma solely among children with above-median ETV (adjusted OR = 1.63; 95% CI, 1.14–2.33) in the full cohort.
Among lifetime residents with less exposure measurement error, the association was magnified (adjusted OR = 2.40; 95% CI, 1.48–3.88).
The NO2×ETV interaction was statistically significant (p = 0.03) in the full cohort and p = 0.0009 among lifetime residents.
No independent effect of ETV on asthma was found (OR = 0.98; 95% CI, 0.78–1.22).
Among children with below-median ETV, there was no association between NO2 and asthma (OR = 0.94; 95% CI, 0.70–1.26).
captured_features: Retrospectively estimated residential NO2 exposure (year-of-diagnosis, 1-SD = 4.3 ppb)
Rasch-scored lifetime exposure to violence (ETV) from caregiver questionnaire
Parent-reported asthma diagnosis and asthmatic bronchitis
population: 413 children (from 888 live births) in East Boston, Massachusetts, recruited 1987–1993 and assessed via questionnaire at ages 4–11.5 years
exposure_domain: Traffic-related air pollution (NO2) and exposure to violence (social stressor)
limitations: Small sample size limited power to investigate multiplicative interaction effects.
NO2 used as a marker of vehicular emissions may not represent all pollutants of interest.
Incomplete residential history likely introduced nondifferential exposure misclassification.
Retrospective caregiver report of violence is subject to recall and reporting (underreporting) bias.
ETV may proxy for other unmeasured social stressors and indoor exposures.
